title: A Complex Story: Universal Preference vs. Individual Differences Shaping Aesthetic Response to Fractals Patterns
research_question: To test preference responses to Fractal Dimension (FD) and visual complexity, using a large cohort of participants from around the world, and to explore the extent to which age, culture, and gender can predict preferences for fractally complex patterns.

participants.description: 228 men and 204 women, aged between 17 and 88 (M = 31.03, SD = 14.45). Participants were from four continent locations: Europe (n = 177), North America (n = 24), Central Asia (n = 195), and Africa (n = 97).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 81 abstract monochrome fractal images (9 full sets of 9 iterations of Fractal Dimension, FD) generated using the mid-point displacement technique. All stimuli were developed in bitmap format.

measures.instrument: Two alternative forced choice (57 stimulus pairs)
Inherent property of generated fractal images (D1.1-D1.9)
GIF compression based on measures by Forsythe et al. (2003), specifically GIF Ratio score (higher GIF ratio = lower complexity)
Self-report of Age, Gender, and Continent of residence

findings.consequent: GIF ratio (measure of visual complexity)
findings.mechanism: Fractal dimension is strongly negatively correlated with GIF ratio, indicating that images with higher FD are more visually complex.
findings.quote: The results of this exploration show a strong negative correlation between FD and the GIF ratio complexity measure (r(79) = -0.93, p < 0.01)

findings.consequent: aesthetic preference rating
findings.mechanism: Overall preference patterns showed a peak at D1.2 (M = 6.89, SD = 3.89) and lowest at D1.8 (M = 4.69, SD = 3.89).
findings.quote: The results show that there was a significant effect of FD, (F(1.467, 777.46) = 35.06, p < 0.001, η² = 0.06).

findings.antecedent: Fractal Dimension (FD) and continent of residence
findings.consequent: aesthetic preference rating
findings.mechanism: Preference ratings differed significantly between FD and location grouping. North American samples showed a negative linear preference, differing from the suggested positive direction in European, Central Asian, and African samples.
findings.quote: The results show that there was a significant effect of FD and location grouping (F(4.42,720.6) = 4.00, p < 0.001, η² = 0.02).

findings.consequent: aesthetic preference rating
findings.mechanism: Male preference peaked at D1.2 (M = 7.32, SD = 3.94) and decreased as FD increased, showing a low-to-mid peak. Female preference peaked at D1.6 (M = 6.58, SD = 1.88) with less variation.
findings.quote: Male preference peaks at D1.2 (M = 7.32, SD = 3.94) and continues to fall as FD increases from this point. ... Female preference peaks at D1.6 (M = 6.58, SD = 1.88)

findings.consequent: aesthetic preference rating
findings.mechanism: Males showed significantly higher preference for D1.1 fractals compared to females.
findings.quote: significant differences were found across D1.1 (t(528) = 2.68, p < 0.01)

findings.consequent: aesthetic preference rating
findings.mechanism: Males showed significantly higher preference for D1.2 fractals compared to females.

findings.consequent: aesthetic preference rating
findings.mechanism: Males showed significantly higher preference for D1.3 fractals compared to females.

findings.consequent: aesthetic preference rating
findings.mechanism: Females showed significantly higher preference for D1.6 fractals compared to males.

findings.consequent: aesthetic preference rating
findings.mechanism: Females showed significantly higher preference for D1.8 fractals compared to males.

findings.consequent: aesthetic preference rating
findings.mechanism: Females showed significantly higher preference for D1.9 fractals compared to males.

findings.antecedent: Fractal Dimensions D1.4, D1.5, D1.7 and gender
findings.consequent: aesthetic preference rating
findings.mechanism: No significant gender difference in preference was found for D1.4, D1.5, and D1.7 fractals.
findings.quote: no significant difference in preference across D1.4 (t(528) = 1.52, p = 0.129), D1.5 (t(528) = -0.404, p = 0.687) and D1.7 (t(528) = -01.32, p = 0.187)

findings.antecedent: Continent, Gender, and Age (as predictors in a linear mixed-effect model)
findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting the more complex fractal image from a pair
findings.mechanism: The Complexity Model, including Continent, Gender, and Age, significantly improved the prediction of preference for complex fractal patterns compared to a null model.
findings.quote: The complexity model accounts for significantly more variance with fixed and random effects (AIC = 17040, df = 21) than the null model with random effects alone (AIC = 17154, df = 3), suggesting that the model is improved with the additional variables (x(18) = 125.14, p < 0.001).

findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting the more complex fractal image from a pair
findings.mechanism: There was a significant main effect of continent on preference for complex fractal patterns. European participants showed an average 22% choice, African 17%, North American 8%, and Central Asian 3%.
findings.quote: Additional goodness of fit analysis found that Continent (x(15) = 99.06, p < 0.001) significantly improves the overall fit of the model.

findings.antecedent: Continent of residence (European vs. North American)
findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting the more complex fractal image from a pair
findings.mechanism: Significant differences were found between European (22%) and North American (8%) samples in preference for complex fractal images.
findings.quote: Significant differences were however found between European (22%) and North American (8%) samples (β = −1.311, z = -2.601, p < 0.01)

findings.antecedent: Continent of residence (European vs. Central Asian)
findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting the more complex fractal image from a pair
findings.mechanism: Significant differences were found between European (22%) and Central Asian (3%) samples in preference for complex fractal images.
findings.quote: and European (22%) and Central Asian (3%; β = −2.261, z = -8.267, p < 0.001) suggesting individual differences in preference across locations.

findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting the more complex fractal image from a pair
findings.mechanism: Females showed a significantly increased choice in complex fractal shapes (20%) compared with males (5%).
findings.quote: Additional main effects were also found for gender, with females showing a significant increased choice in complex fractal shapes (20%) compared with males (5%; β = 1.585, z = -4.827, p < 0.001).

findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting the more complex fractal image from a pair
findings.mechanism: Age did not significantly add to the overall prediction of preference for complex fractal images.
findings.quote: However, age (x(1) = 6.845, p = 0.445) does not significantly add to the overall prediction of the model.

findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting the more complex fractal image from a pair
findings.mechanism: African males (7%) showed lower probability than African females (27%), and European males (10%) showed lower probability than European females (35%) of choosing the more complex image.
findings.quote: the model shows a significant interaction between continent (Africa-Europe) and gender (β = 1.446, z = 2.64, p < 0.01).

findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting the more complex fractal image from a pair
findings.mechanism: Central Asian males (1%) showed lower probability than Central Asian females (5%), and European males (10%) showed lower probability than European females (35%) of choosing the more complex image.
findings.quote: Interaction effects were also found between Central Asia and Europe and Gender (β = 1.446, z = 2.636, p < 0.01).

findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting the more complex fractal image from a pair
findings.mechanism: Female preference for complexity decreased with age, whereas male preference for complexity increased with age.
findings.quote: A significant interaction was also seen between gender and age (β = 0.028, z = 2.096, p < 0.01). Male and female complexity choices show changes as a function of age. Female participants' preference for complexity decreases with age, whereas male participants' preference for complexity increases with age (Figure 10).

findings.antecedent: Continent, Gender, and Age (as predictors in a linear mixed-effect model)
findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting a mid-range fractal image (1.3-1.5D) from a pair
findings.mechanism: The Mid-Range Model, including Continent, Gender, and Age, significantly improved the prediction of preference for mid-range fractal patterns compared to a null model.
findings.quote: The Mid-Range Model accounts for significantly more variance with fixed and random effects (AIC = 17040, df = 21) than the null model with random effects alone (AIC = 17154, df = 3), suggesting that the model is improved with the additional variables (x(18) = 125.14, p < 0.001).

findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting a mid-range fractal image (1.3-1.5D) from a pair
findings.mechanism: There was a significant main effect of continent on preference for mid-range fractal images. European samples had an average probability of 85%, Central Asia 83%, and North American 89%.
findings.quote: Additional goodness of fit analysis found that Continent (x(15) = 27.89, p < 0.05) improved the overall fit of the model.

findings.antecedent: Continent of residence (European vs. Central Asia)
findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting a mid-range fractal image (1.3-1.5D) from a pair
findings.mechanism: Significant differences were seen between European (85%) and Central Asia (83%) samples in preference for mid-range fractal images.
findings.quote: Significant differences in percentage choices were seen between Europe and Central Asia (β = -0.198, z = -2.262, p < 0.05).

findings.antecedent: Continent of residence (European vs. North American)
findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting a mid-range fractal image (1.3-1.5D) from a pair
findings.mechanism: Marginally significant differences were found between European (85%) and North American (89%) samples in preference for mid-range fractal images.
findings.quote: There are also marginally significant differences in preference choice between European and North American samples (β = -0.339, z = 1.937, p = 0.052).

findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting a mid-range fractal image (1.3-1.5D) from a pair
findings.mechanism: Females (88%) showed an increased probability of choosing mid-range fractal patterns compared with males (86%).
findings.quote: the model found a significant main effect of gender on preference for mid-range fractal images with Females (88%) showing an increased probability of choosing mid-range fractal patterns when compared with males (86%; β = −0.215, z = -2.025, p < 0.05).

findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting a mid-range fractal image (1.3-1.5D) from a pair
findings.mechanism: Age marginally improved the model fit for mid-range preference, but not significantly.
findings.quote: the variable Age marginally improves the model, but not significantly (x(1) = 12.99, p = 0.072)

findings.consequent: likelihood of selecting a mid-range fractal image (1.3-1.5D) from a pair
findings.mechanism: European males (85%) showed lower preference than European females (87%), and Central Asian males (82%) showed lower preference than Central Asian females (85%) for mid-range fractals.
findings.quote: Significant interaction was seen between continent (Central Asia-Europe) and gender (β = 0.299, z = 2.242, p < 0.05), with European males showing a lower preference choice (85%) than European females (87%), and Central Asian males showing a lower choice (82%) than females (85%; see also Figure 11).

mechanisms: Savannah hypothesis (spontaneous emotional responses to landscapes positive for survival, leading to preference for mid-range fractal patterns found in Savannah-type landscapes)
Refuge theory (preference for visual environments offering shelter and ability to move undetected)

Aesthetic development for fractal patterns (innate responses to mid-range fractals, then shaped by repeated exposure to non-mid-range/non-fractal environments, cultural ties, and fluency/exposure hypotheses)

Hunter-gatherer hypothesis (sex differences in spatial abilities due to division of labor: foraging for females requiring understanding complex scenes, hunting for males requiring coordinated spatial relations)
Processing fluency (ease of processing leads to aesthetic pleasure)
Familiarity effects (previous exposure influencing perception of complexity and aesthetic preference)
implementation_implications: The fragility of universal aesthetic claims for fractal patterns is highlighted, suggesting that individual differences in preference for visual complexity across culture, gender, and age should be considered in design.
limitations: The dichotomous forced-choice design with pure fractal imagery, while controlling for familiarity, is not ideal for understanding real-world preference.
The study acknowledges that macro visual environment differences across continents may have some, but limited, differences across the locations used.
Further investigation is needed into the effect of micro or sub-cultural environments (e.g., urban and rural landscapes) on preference.
Neuropsychological measures were not used to support hypotheses regarding neural differences in gender-based spatial processing.
